transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-06-09
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Hightide Head of ML), Tom Becker (Hightide Infra), Lina Morales (Hightide CTO), Evan (Hightide SRE)
---
Summary: quick scrub of this week's benchmark runs comparing Redwood pilot vs incumbent (IncumbentAI). Focus on latency tail, throughput under burst, and unit cost delta. Agreed next steps include a 1M-token head-to-head and canary scheduling.
Topics: results overview, p95/p99 tail, batching and kv cache tuning, routing and fallback, cost per 1k tokens, dedicated slot sizing.
---
[00:00] Maya: okay folks, thanks for joining, quick agenda — we want to walk through the lab runs from this week, called out the head-to-head vs IncumbentAI, highlight where we've improved and where we still see tail spikes. we have Diego to run the deep numbers.
[00:23] Diego: yep hi everyone. pushing screen — i'm going to summarize the run matrix: three patterns — steady low qps, steady high qps, and bursty day (hour-long spikes). For each we did Redwood hosted baseline, Redwood quantized (int8-ish), and the incumbent.
[00:45] Priya: quick Q — are these using the same tokenization/temperature and the exact same prompts as our baseline? last time a mismatch caused a 10% throughput delta.
[00:58] Noah: good call. we normalized prompt set; some mild differences in sampling were re-aligned. we trimmed padding and matched batch composition — should be apples-to-apples within noise.
[01:14] Tom: the numbers we care about: p50/p95/p99 for latency and throughput in rps and tokens/sec — also unit-cost per 1K tokens.
[01:25] Diego: right — for steady-high (200 rps equivalent): Redwood hosted quantized was p50 48ms, p95 128ms, p99 260ms. Incumbent p50 42ms, p95 140ms, p99 520ms. so we beat incumbents on p99 by a wide margin in quantized path. (note: transcription occasionally says "quantisize" — meant quantization).
[01:56] Lina: wow p99 520ms for incumbent — that's pretty bad under tail. what about throughput?
[02:07] Diego: throughput per GPU: Redwood sustained 600 tokens/sec steady across our model shard, incumbent peaked then dipped under burst. under the burst pattern (1-minute spikes to 800 rps), the incumbent had a 30% drop in sustained tokens/sec, while Redwood's routing + cache had a 12% drop.
[02:30] Evan: are you using KV cache advantages for repeated prefixes? our traffic has lots of repeated system prompts so cache should help.
[02:40] Diego: yes, we enabled KV cache for repeated contexts. note — sometimes the export logs label it "KV cash" (minor transcription error) but it's the same. Cache cut token compute by ~18% on average for our workload.
[02:56] Priya: cost numbers — what was the cost delta per 1K tokens? we need to show finance.
[03:03] Maya: summary first: raw unit cost (hosted, quantized) was about $0.85 per 1K tokens vs incumbent $1.10 per 1K. With Dedicated reserved slots (per our estimate) we can get to roughly $0.60 per 1K depending on commit and burst policy.
[03:20] Priya: okay that helps. but finance also cares about SLO breaches — our SLA target is <150ms p95 for end-to-end user. are we meeting that in production-like bursts?
[03:31] Diego: in the staging runs with Redwood hosted quantized we met p95 128ms under steady-high, but under the worst-case burst scenario we saw a few p95 excursions to ~190ms primarily at the start of burst while autoscaler spin-up happened. the mitigation is to use dedicated reserved slots or pre-warm burst capacity.
[03:57] Tom: how fast is autoscaling in your hosted offering? we need to know ramp times.
[04:03] Noah: typical warm-up is 60–120s depending on instance type and model size. we can configure warm standby (burst buffer) to reduce that. for real-time user SLOs, customers often use a small reserved baseline to avoid cold-surge latency.
[04:22] Priya: if we go dedicated, what's recommended for our traffic — 2 GPUs or 4? our peak is about 800 interactive rps for a northern-eu region during morning shift.
[04:33] Diego: based on current bench, for 800 rps with 95th percentile headroom we recommend starting with 2x A100-equivalent slots and add a burst slot. but if you need a hard 150ms p95 under sustained bursts, 4 dedicated will be safer. we can optimize kernels and quantize more aggressively to reduce that to 3 GPUs.
[04:56] Lina: any functional differences between the quantized path and the float path we need to flag for accuracy/regression? we can't have hallucination regressions.
[05:04] Diego: we ran the eval set — quantized path had negligible delta on Rouge/Exact Match for our prompt set (within 0.6% absolute). we'll attach evals in the report. caveat: some rare long-context cases see slight shift; we recommend keeping full precision for those routes.
[05:25] Priya: also tell me about routing — you mentioned fallback policies earlier. how deterministic are those?
[05:31] Maya: Redwood supports routing policies by latency or cost. you can configure a priority list: primary model, fallback lower-cost variant, fallback to other region. automatic fallback kicks in when queue latency exceeds threshold. it's deterministic but configurable.
[05:47] Evan: logs — we need token-level traces and sampling of requests to match to user sessions for debugging — do you provide those?
[05:54] Noah: yes — per-route traces, request ids, and token timing are available. sensitive fields can be redacted before shipping to logs. we can integrate with your KMS for encryption at rest.
[06:06] Tom: security question — SOC2 and ISO? also we run in a VPC for some PII flows. can you deploy private?
[06:13] Maya: Redwood Private is possible — we have a VPC-deployed control plane and on-prem options. SOC2 Type II in process, we have ISO docs requested — we'll share the current compliance pack.
[06:24] Lina: great. back to bench: what caused the p99 tail improvement on Redwood vs incumbent? is it kernel selection, batching, or routing?
[06:33] Diego: three factors: (1) continuous batching with adaptive thresholds reduced small-batch overhead, (2) optimized kernels for attention pattern we use, (3) proactive KV cache hits and routing that prioritize latency SLO traffic. incumbent had higher p50 but much higher variance and less aggressive tail control.
[06:52] Priya: any risks we should be tracking for the next run?
[06:55] Diego: risk: synthetic lab environment might under-represent cross-tenant noisy neighbor effects; mitigation: run the head-to-head in a stager that mimics background noise, and we'll also run a mix with real sampled traffic you provide.
[07:10] Maya: ok let's go through concrete next steps — Diego will run the 1M-token head-to-head with the burst profile (Priya to send traffic sample). we'll include p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU utilization, batching histogram, and distribution of KV cache hit rates.
[07:26] Priya: timeline sounds good. one more ask — can you show the cost ladder if we do hybrid: hosted for off-peak, dedicated for peak? finance likes blended metrics.
[07:36] Maya: yes we'll prepare blended cost modeling and show break-even points for commit levels.
[07:41] Tom: on instrumentation, Evan will need the tracing pointers.
[07:45] Evan: i'll send a list of the fields we need to correlate by EOD tomorrow.
[07:50] Speaker 3: (mumbled) i also noted some noise in the logs where the batch size jumped — we should look at the autoscaler thresholds.
[07:59] Diego: good flag — autoscaler thresholds and target queue length will be part of the runbook we share.
[08:07] Priya: final — surprised by the cost improvement but happy to see tail gains. i'm still wary of that autoscaler spin up causing p95 blips.
[08:16] Maya: understood. for pilot we can recommend keep a small baseline dedicated capacity to meet your 150ms p95. we'll include a canary playbook for cutover with traffic percent steps.
[08:28] Noah: i'll also include a short section on quantization caveats and how to route long context to non-quantized models automatically.
[08:36] Priya: perfect.
[08:38] Maya: ok let's recap action items quickly: Diego runs head-to-head, Priya shares traffic, Maya sends pricing and compliance docs, and we schedule the canary. thanks everyone.
